opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is that people really need to be bilingual, and I mean that in a deep sense, not just picking up a few terms from the other field. When I started working in this area, a lot of the computational work was done by people who were very strong in machine learning but treated biology as just another source of data, and a lot of the biology was done by people who saw computation as a service, something you hand off at the end. Neither of those really works for the hard problems.

So for students in my lab, I encourage them to get a genuinely solid foundation in machine learning and the core principles, things like probabilistic modeling, optimization, and now increasingly explainability and interpretability, because those give you the tools to ask new kinds of questions. But at the same time, they have to spend real time understanding the biology and the clinical context. What does a gene expression measurement actually mean? How is that data generated, and what are the biases and batch effects? In medicine, what decision is a clinician actually making, and what would they need to trust a model's output? If you don't understand that, you can build a model that's very accurate on a benchmark and completely useless, or even harmful, in practice.

Collaboration is a big part of the training too. I think students should work closely with biologists and physicians from early on, sitting in their meetings, going to clinical conferences, not just computer science venues. Some of our most interesting projects came from a clinician saying, "I don't trust this black box, I need to know why it's making this prediction." That pushed us toward explainable AI methods, and those methods ended up leading to new biological insights, for example identifying which features or genes are driving a prediction, which you can then test experimentally.

Finally, I'd say students should be trained to care about the problem first rather than the method. In machine learning there's a temptation to develop a fancier model and then look for a dataset. In biomedicine, the most impactful work usually starts from an important question, like why some patients respond to a cancer drug and others don't, or how we can detect disease earlier, and then you develop or adapt methods to answer it. If students learn to think that way, being rigorous on the computational side and humble and curious on the biological side, I think they're in a great position to really advance the field.

r001.rationale: The response advocates deep fluency in machine learning, biology, and clinical context, including learning how clinicians make decisions and collaborating directly with biologists and physicians.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks so much for having me. This is a question I think about constantly, because my own path was anything but linear. I was trained as a computer scientist, I did my PhD in machine learning, and then I had to essentially go back to school in my own head to understand enough biology and medicine to ask questions that actually matter to clinicians and biologists. So a lot of my thinking comes from the gaps I had to fill myself.

The first thing I'd say is that you really need deep training in one discipline. I don't believe in the model where someone learns a little bit of everything and becomes a sort of generalist from day one. The problems at this intersection are hard precisely because each field has its own depth. If you want to develop new methods, you need to genuinely understand statistics, optimization, how models fail, where the assumptions break. If you're coming from the biology side, you need to deeply understand the experimental systems, what the measurements mean, where the noise comes from. So depth first.

But then, and this is the part that I think is often neglected, you need enough fluency in the other domain to recognize when a problem is real. That doesn't mean becoming a biologist if you're a computer scientist. It means being able to read a biology paper, follow a clinical conversation, and most importantly, be able to tell the difference between a problem that a biologist cares about and a problem that just looks interesting from a machine learning perspective. I've seen a lot of beautiful methods applied to datasets where the underlying biological question was never clearly articulated, and the results end up not mattering to anyone.

The way we try to do this in my lab is to insist on genuine collaboration, not consultation. My students talk to clinicians and wet lab biologists regularly, not just when they need a dataset or a sanity check at the end. When you sit in on a tumor board, or watch how a pathologist actually makes a call, or hear a biologist describe why an experiment failed, it changes what you think the interesting questions are. Computational researchers often assume the hard part is the prediction. Very often the hard part is figuring out what the right prediction target even is, or realizing that nobody will trust a model they can't interrogate.

That brings me to something I feel strongly about, which is that students should be trained to take interpretability and the downstream human seriously from the beginning. In medicine, a model that gets a high AUC but can't explain itself, or that learns a shortcut like which hospital the data came from, isn't just less useful, it can be harmful. So I want students to think about who will use this, what decision it informs, and how we would know if it was wrong. That mindset is a form of training, and it's not something you pick up from a standard machine learning curriculum.

Practically, I think PhD programs could do more to create structured space for this. Co-advising across departments is extremely valuable. Rotations in a lab or clinic for computational students. Letting biology and medical trainees take real courses in machine learning rather than a watered-down version. And honestly, giving people permission to be slow at first. When you're learning a second field, you feel incompetent for a while, and students in competitive programs don't like feeling incompetent. Advisors need to protect that period.

The last thing I'd say is that this intersection rewards humility and patience. The fields move at different speeds, publish in different ways, and value different things. A computational person wants a clean result; a clinician wants something that works on Tuesday morning in the clinic with messy data. Learning to hold both of those standards at once, and to communicate across them, is probably the single most important skill. It's not something you can teach in a semester, but you can build training environments where people are constantly practicing it.

r001.rationale: The response advocates deep grounding in one field alongside fluency in other domains, regular collaboration with clinicians and biologists, and learning to hold computational and clinical standards together. This communicates training researchers to integrate perspectives from machine learning, biology, and medicine.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to train researchers to formulate questions across disciplines, rather than simply giving them a collection of courses in computer science, biology, and medicine. They need depth in a particular area, but also enough understanding of the other fields to recognize which problems matter and what would count as a meaningful answer.

For example, when a computer scientist works with a clinician, improving a model’s prediction accuracy may be only one part of the problem. What decision would that prediction inform? What does the data actually measure? Could the model be learning something about how patients receive care rather than something about their biology? Those questions should shape the computational work from the beginning.

So I would emphasize working closely with people from other disciplines early in training. Students need practice asking basic questions, explaining their assumptions, and being comfortable saying, “I don’t understand.” The goal is to develop researchers who can connect a computational method to a biological or clinical question and then critically evaluate whether it really helps answer that question.

r001.rationale: The response advocates training researchers to connect computational methods with biological and clinical questions, and to work closely with people from other disciplines early in training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think researchers need depth in one discipline, but also enough understanding of the others to ask meaningful questions and collaborate effectively. It’s not realistic to expect everyone to become an expert in computer science, biology, and medicine. But a computer scientist should understand the biological question, how the data were generated, and what a result would mean in a clinical setting.

I would make that part of training early on. Give students opportunities to work closely with biologists and clinicians, and to spend time understanding their questions before developing a method. Those conversations can be challenging because we use different language and make different assumptions. Learning to recognize those differences is an important research skill.

And I would encourage students to keep asking: If our method works, what will we learn? How could we validate that finding? That helps connect computational advances to discoveries that matter in biology and medicine.

r001.rationale: The response advocates depth in one discipline and enough cross-disciplinary understanding to collaborate and connect methods to biological and clinical questions. It does not clearly advocate integrating expert ways of thinking across machine learning, biology, and clinical medicine; it explicitly says researchers need not become experts in all three.
